The Wikimedia credit is retained in the attribution footer, which also discloses the substitution. This is a deliberate local replacement, not a transcription of the source figure: do not reverse it toward the composite in a later audit.

It substituted $(0,0)$ into $x + 2y$ for the system $3x + y = 0, x + 2y = -5$, where the point satisfies the first equation but not the second — the pedagogical point — but the answer $0$ is also the substituted value, so a learner reading $x = 0$ off the prompt is graded correct, and the zero also hides the arithmetic behind the multiply-by-zero shortcut. metadataDecisions.rationale: The fluorochrome example sentence says Texas red is excited by blue light and FITC absorbs invisible ultraviolet light. Manufacturer spectral data (Thermo Fisher Molecular Probes Handbook: Texas Red sulfonyl chloride absorption 588 nm; fluorescein/FITC peak excitation 488-495 nm) place Texas red's excitation in the orange and FITC's in the visible blue. The local sentence states orange and blue, carries a visible Source note, and the footer discloses the change. Found by the prose claim pass, September 6, 2026.

The source dates the Athenian plague 'between 430 and 410 BC'. Thucydides describes the outbreak of 430 BC and its recurrence ending in 426 BC, and the modern review (Littman, Mount Sinai Journal of Medicine 76 [2009]: 456-467, doi:10.1002/msj.20137) dates it 430-426 BC; no source supports 410. The local page prints 426 BC with a visible Source note and footer disclosure. Found by the prose claim pass, September 6, 2026.

The source says Haloquadratum walsbyi cells 'are arranged in square clusters of four cells'. The primary morphology paper (Bolhuis et al., 'Morphological and Structural Aspects of the Extremely Halophilic Archaeon Haloquadratum walsbyi', PMC3084702) describes flat square cells joined in fragile postage-stamp sheets, not fixed quartets; the genus name refers to the square cell shape. The local page says sheets of square cells with a visible Source note and footer disclosure. Found by the prose claim pass, September 6, 2026.

The prose dates John Snow's water-source cholera study to 1848 while the same module's timeline figure dates it to 1854, the year of the Broad Street and water-company investigations. The page follows the module's own figure, with a visible Source note and footer disclosure. Found by the prose claim pass, September 6, 2026.

The Ions paragraph gives sodium 11 neutrons and chlorine 17 neutrons. Sodium is monoisotopic (sodium-23: 11 protons, 12 neutrons; NIST Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions), and the same module's Atomic Number and Mass paragraph gives chlorine's majority isotope 17 protons and 18 neutrons, so the Ions paragraph contradicts its own section. The local page prints 12 and 18 with a visible Source note and discloses the change in its footer. Found by the prose claim pass sample, September 6, 2026. ALSO (erratum 376): The Carbon Dating box says carbon-14 decays to nitrogen-14 'by a process called beta decay-electrons or positrons emission.' Carbon-14 decays 100% by beta-minus (electron) emission to nitrogen-14 (LNHB Table de Radionucleides; NNDC/ENSDF); positron emission would lower the atomic number, not raise it to nitrogen. The local page says electron emission with a visible Source note and footer disclosure. Found by the prose claim pass sample, September 6, 2026.

The source says Golgi observed the stacked membranes in Plasmodium cells. Golgi's 1898 communication described the internal reticular apparatus in neurons of the cerebellum and spinal ganglia (Bentivoglio et al., Frontiers in Neuroanatomy 13 [2019], doi:10.3389/fnana.2019.00003); his malaria work was separate. The page says nerve cells with a visible Source note and footer disclosure. Found by the prose claim pass, September 6, 2026. ALSO (erratum 381): The source dates de Duve's discovery of lysosomes to the 1960s. The primary paper is de Duve et al., Biochemical Journal 60 (1955): 604-617; the 1960s work was peroxisomes (Bonetta, Journal of Cell Biology 169 [2005]: 705, doi:10.1083/jcb1695fta2). The page says 1955 with a visible Source note and footer disclosure. Found by the prose claim pass, September 6, 2026.

The page reads "A recombinant chimeric live attenuated vaccine against Japanese encephalitis virus--not a DNA vaccine--was approved for use in humans in 2010 in Australia" with a visible Source note citing the TGA listing and the PMC review (erratum 626). No item, hint, or key term on the page was built on the old wording. Found by the chapter 18 prose claim pass, September 13, 2026.

"Phylogenetic diversity of the Rickettsiae." Journal of Bacteriology 171, no. 8 (1989): 4202-4206), matching the book's own Gammaproteobacteria table rather than the "rickettsia" label used in this section. It can generate hydrogen peroxide, which may adversely affect host cell membranes through the production of reactive oxygen species," attributing hydrogen-peroxide generation to the protease enzyme itself. In the Ureaplasma virulence-factor literature, IgA protease activity and hydrogen-peroxide production are documented as separate factors of the organism, not one enzyme performing both. The page reads "*U. urealyticum* can also generate hydrogen peroxide, which may adversely affect host cell membranes through the production of reactive oxygen species" with a visible Source note beside the passage (erratum 721). The Genital Herpes subsection's latency paragraph reads "The virus moves down peripheral nerves, typically sensory neurons, to ganglia in the spine (either the trigeminal ganglion or the lumbar-sacral ganglia) and becomes latent," grouping the trigeminal ganglion under "ganglia in the spine." The trigeminal ganglion (Gasserian/semilunar ganglion) is a cranial nerve ganglion seated in Meckel's cave of the middle cranial fossa, inside the skull -- not in the spine; only the lumbar-sacral (dorsal root) ganglia are actually spinal. This book's own sibling modules never call the trigeminal ganglion spinal: m58908 (Section 21.3, HSV-1 latency) describes it as "residing in the trigeminal nerve ganglia" with no spinal claim, m58940 (CNS infections) treats the trigeminal nerve as a distinct non-spinal cranial route into the CNS, and m58914 (varicella-zoster) correctly confines "the spine" language to VZV's actual dorsal ganglia. The page reads "sensory ganglia (either the trigeminal ganglion, in the head, or the lumbar-sacral ganglia, in the spine)" with a visible Source note beside the passage (erratum 720). No item, hint, or key term on the page was built on the old wording. Found by the chapter 23 prose claim pass, September 14, 2026.

The Tick Tips Micro Connection box's anatomy sentence reads "Adult ticks have eight legs and two body segments, the cephalothorax and the head," printed exactly as quoted. A cephalothorax is by definition a fused head-and-thorax tagma, so naming "the cephalothorax and the head" as two separate segments is internally contradictory, and ticks (order Ixodida, class Arachnida) do not have a cephalothorax at all -- their two body regions are the capitulum (gnathosoma, bearing the mouthparts) and the idiosoma (bearing the leg pairs and housing the digestive/reproductive organs), unlike spiders and other arachnids, which do have a true cephalothorax plus abdomen. This book is silent on tick anatomy terminology elsewhere, so external references were used to confirm the correction: WikiVet, "Tick Morphology" ("Ticks have two body regions: a very large idiosoma... and a much smaller anterior gnathosoma (also called the capitulum)"), and Medicine LibreTexts, "10.2: General anatomy of ticks" ("Tagmatization in acarines is reduced to two unique tagmata with no distinction between the more conventional cephalothorax and abdomen"). The page's Tick Tips box reads "Adult ticks have eight legs and two body regions, the capitulum, which bears the mouthparts, and the idiosoma" with a visible Source note beside the correction (erratum 765), on the same footing as chapter 23's and 24's visible-Source-note corrections (errata 719-721, 751, 766). The HIV subsection's opening sentence (para fs-id1167663742703) reads "Human T-lymphotropic viruses (HTLV), also called human immunodeficiency viruses (HIV) are retroviruses that are the causative agent of acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS)," presenting HTLV and HIV as alternate names for the same virus. They are distinct human retroviruses in family Retroviridae, subfamily Orthoretrovirinae, but different genera -- HTLV-1/HTLV-2 in genus Deltaretrovirus, HIV-1/HIV-2 in genus Lentivirus -- with different replication strategies (deltaretroviruses replicate chiefly by driving infected-cell division; lentiviruses like HIV replicate mainly by producing progeny virions) and different disease associations (HTLV causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma and HAM/TSP, not AIDS). This book is silent on HTLV elsewhere -- no sibling module names it, so the false equivalence is not internally self-contradicted -- but it is a citable factual error: ICTV Retroviridae taxonomy (https://ictv.global/report/chapter/retroviridae/taxonomy/retroviridae) places Deltaretrovirus and Lentivirus as distinct genera of subfamily Orthoretrovirinae, and PMC9505669 describes their divergent replication biology.
